text: Genesis places seed-bearing vegetation on day three (1:11–13) and the heavenly lights on day four (1:14–19). Reading these as the first physical appearance of plants and the Sun reverses the order in the accepted solar-system formation model.
scope: The strongest disagreement is the Sun–Earth–plants sequence under a literal first-creation reading. A literary arrangement, later visibility of an existing Sun, or miraculous light changes the claim being evaluated; these readings are not established by the scientific sources. Science models natural processes and cannot independently test an unspecified miracle.
summary: On a literal timeline, plants appear before the Sun. Science places the Sun before Earth and its plants.

fields.text: The Sun formed from a collapsing gas-and-dust cloud; planets formed from material in the surrounding disk. Earth’s plants therefore came after the Sun, not before it. This is a conflict about the sequence of natural events, not merely the length of a “day.”

Photosynthesis uses light energy to make sugars from carbon dioxide and water. A naturally developing plant ecosystem needs an energy source. However, Genesis 1:3 already describes light: photosynthesis alone does not prove these plants were in total darkness or that sunlight is the only possible light source.

text: The Sun helps mark days and years; the yearly seasonal cycle relates to Earth’s tilted axis and orbit.
scope: Agreement with observable cycles does not establish the chapter’s creation sequence.
summary: The Sun helps mark days and years. Earth’s tilt and orbit explain the seasonal cycle.

fields.text: Earth’s rotation produces the day–night cycle, and its orbit around the Sun provides the basis of the solar year. These regular motions support the broad observation that heavenly lights can mark time.
The seasonal cycle depends on Earth’s axial tilt as it orbits the Sun. This agreement concerns observable cycles, not the chapter’s order of creation.

text: The day–night pattern broadly agrees with Earth rotating so different regions face toward or away from the Sun.
scope: This is agreement with the observed pattern, not evidence that every detail of the account is scientific.
summary: The day–night pattern agrees with Earth rotating toward and away from the Sun.

fields.text: On a rotating Earth, the side facing the Sun receives daylight and the side turned away experiences night. The verse’s distinction between day and night agrees with this observed pattern; it does not explain the rotation mechanism.

text: If “not be removed” means Earth is physically motionless, that conflicts with Earth’s rotation and orbit around the Sun.
scope: The passage is poetry. Stability or permanence is another reading; the disagreement applies to physical immobility.
summary: If this poem means Earth never moves, it conflicts with Earth’s rotation and orbit. Stability is another possible meaning.

fields.text: Earth spins on its axis and moves around the Sun. A claim that Earth is physically motionless would contradict both motions. The verse is poetry, however: permanence or stability need not mean zero motion.

text: River water reaches the sea and circulates through the water cycle by evaporation, precipitation, and runoff.
scope: Broad observational agreement; the verse does not provide a complete hydrological explanation.
summary: Rivers flowing to the sea broadly fit the water cycle, though the verse does not explain the full process.

fields.text: Water moves through rivers to the ocean and returns to land through evaporation, atmospheric transport and precipitation. This circulation explains why continued river flow does not simply fill the sea without any return process.

text: The image of water rising and returning as rain broadly aligns with evaporation, condensation, and precipitation.
scope: A poetic description, not a complete scientific model.
summary: The poetic description of water rising and returning as rain broadly fits the water cycle.

fields.text: Water evaporates, moves through the atmosphere, condenses and returns as precipitation. The rising-water and rain imagery broadly resembles that circulation. The poem does not specify the complete mechanisms, so this is observational agreement rather than a scientific theory.

text: Josephus describes Herod as a historical ruler of Judea.
scope: Corroborates the ruler and setting; does not independently establish Jesus’s birth or the visit of the magi.
summary: Josephus confirms Herod ruled Judea. This supports the setting, not the birth story itself.

text: Josephus describes Archelaus succeeding Herod and receiving authority over Judea.
scope: Supports the succession. Archelaus’s formal Roman title was ethnarch; it does not independently verify the family’s journey.
summary: Josephus confirms Archelaus succeeded Herod in Judea. This supports the succession, not the family’s journey.

text: Josephus places the census under Quirinius after Archelaus’s removal, which came after Herod’s death. This conflicts with placing that same census in the Herod-era birth setting.
scope: A chronological tension assuming this is the census Josephus describes. Other proposed readings require additional evidence.
summary: Josephus places Quirinius’s census after Herod’s death. Using that census for a Herod-era birth creates a chronological conflict.

text: Josephus records Pilate governing Judea under Tiberius.
scope: Supports those officials and their setting; does not verify every date, title, or named ruler in this verse.
summary: Josephus records Pilate governing Judea under Tiberius. This supports those officials and the setting.

text: Josephus also describes Judas the Galilean’s opposition to the census under Quirinius.
scope: Supports the existence of a census-related movement, not every detail of its leader’s death or followers’ dispersal.
summary: Josephus also describes Judas the Galilean opposing Quirinius’s census. This supports the movement, not every detail of the verse.

title: A solid sky dome?
summary: A literal solid dome holding back an upper sea conflicts with atmospheric science. Whether “firmament” means that dome is an interpretive question.
text: Genesis 1:6–7 describes a divider between waters below and waters above. Paul H. Seely argues that the Hebrew term refers to a solid sky; Vern S. Poythress instead reads the upper waters as rain-bearing clouds. The science comparison below evaluates the solid-dome interpretation, not every possible meaning of the verse.

fields.text: Earth’s atmosphere has gaseous layers that become increasingly thin toward space. A rigid roof enclosing the sky and supporting an upper ocean is incompatible with that measured structure.

Clouds and almost all atmospheric water vapor occur in the lower atmosphere. That differs from a cosmic ocean retained above a solid sky barrier. Water in clouds does not, by itself, conflict with science.

scope: “Snowglobe Earth” is a modern analogy for the dome interpretation, not a phrase or complete model stated in this verse. Verse 6 alone does not establish a flat Earth. The physical dome model disagrees with science; the lexical and literary interpretation remains disputed. This is our conditional assessment, not a NASA judgment on scripture.
